canonical_name: Wallace H. Coulter 1953 Impedance Particle/Cell Counting Patent (Coulter Principle)
creator: Wallace H. Coulter (assigned later to Coulter Electronics, now Beckman Coulter / Danaher)
disclosure_citation: Coulter, W.H. US patent application filed 1949-10-20, US2656508A issued 1953-10-20, 'Means for counting particles suspended in a fluid'; Coulter, W.H. 'High speed automatic blood cell counter and cell size analyzer,' Proc. National Electronics Conference vol. 12 pp. 1034-1042 (1956)
end_application: automated cell counting (RBC, WBC, PLT in human and veterinary hematology); particle size analysis (industrial powders, paints, pharmaceutical APIs); foundational technology for ALL impedance-based hematology analyzers (Beckman Coulter, Sysmex, Mindray, IDEXX, Abbott Cell-Dyn, Nihon Kohden, etc.)
fabrication_method: precision-drilled aperture (~50-200 µm in original; 50-100 µm typical for blood cells; sub-µm for nanoparticle Coulter variants today) in a glass or sapphire wafer between two electrolyte chambers
flow_regime: constant-current or constant-voltage applied across aperture; particles suspended in electrolyte are pulled through aperture by pressure or flow; each particle displaces electrolyte volume equal to its own volume, momentarily increasing aperture impedance, producing a voltage pulse whose amplitude is proportional to particle volume
notable_capabilities: volume-resolved single-particle counting
throughput thousands of particles/second
electrolyte-conductivity-only requirement (no labels, no optics required)
extension to sub-micron via tunable resistive pulse sensing (TRPS, npore Coulter variant)
prior_art_notes: Discloses the foundational electrical-sensing-zone (Coulter principle) particle/cell counting technique: an electrolyte-filled chamber is divided by a small aperture (microfluidic constriction) bridged by an applied DC current; particles passing through the aperture displace electrolyte volume, momentarily increasing aperture impedance and producing voltage pulses whose amplitude is proportional to particle volume. Anticipates: ALL subsequent impedance-based microfluidic cell/particle counters (Coulter Counter Z series, all hematology analyzers using impedance, sub-µm 'tunable resistive pulse sensing' nanopore variants, microfluidic on-chip impedance cytometry). The 1953 patent expired in 1971 (17-year US term at the time), placing the foundational technique in the public domain — but downstream design improvements (sapphire apertures, hybrid optical-impedance, sweep-flow geometry) remain patented in modern instruments. This entry serves as the historical anchor making clear that any modern microfluidic impedance counter has 70+ years of expired-patent prior art to draw on.
sources: Coulter, W.H. Proc. National Electronics Conference 12:1034-1042 (1956)
Graham, M.D. 'The Coulter Principle: Foundation of an Industry,' JALA 8(6):72-81 (2003)
substrate_material: glass aperture (originally drilled in mica or glass); electrolyte (saline) on both sides of aperture; platinum electrodes on each side

This is the cluster-generation chemistry at the heart of every Illumina flowcell. Solexa licensed it from Manteia in 2004; Illumina acquired Solexa (and the licensed Manteia rights) in 2007. The Manteia priority date (April 1997) is the earliest critical date for solid-phase clonal-cluster amplification, prior art against any later clusters-on-a-surface or polony claim. Closely related to and roughly contemporaneous with Mitra and Church polony (polymerase colony) work; the corpus records both to map the surface-clonal-amplification prior art landscape. Anticipates: bentley-2008-illumina-flow-cell, Complete Genomics patterned arrays, Element AVITI surface chemistry.
sample_volume: microliter reagent exchange over a planar grafted surface

IP.com Prior Art Database is a paid service where companies file defensive disclosures to establish 102 prior-art dates. The service is examined by USPTO and EPO as non-patent literature (NPL). The Free Microfluidics Corpus is similar in defensive function but differs in: (a) being CC0 / public domain; (b) being free; (c) being domain-specific to microfluidics; (d) using RFC 3161 + OpenTimestamps anchoring rather than IP.com's custodial timestamping. This entry exists for completeness — defensive-publication infrastructure should itself be cataloged as part of the patent-thicket landscape this corpus documents. claims-only disclosure with no working device shown to FDA validation
notes: Reassigned post-bankruptcy to Fortress Investment Group; Fortress sued BioFire in 2020 using these patents during the COVID-19 emergency.
prior_art_notes: Theranos cartridge patent family. Anchors claims around: (a) handheld disposable diagnostic cartridge accepting finger-stick blood; (b) integrated reagent-storage, sample-prep, and detection chambers; (c) on-cartridge assay scheduling and barcode identification; (d) wireless data return to a central reader. Notable for two reasons: (1) the patents were granted but the corresponding products never demonstrated the claimed performance (FDA correspondence and later trial testimony established this); (2) post-bankruptcy the patents were reassigned to Fortress Investment Group / Labrador Diagnostics, which asserted them against working diagnostic companies (notably BioFire) during the COVID pandemic, drawing significant criticism. Defensive value is high: Theranos patent disclosures contain extensive claim language but minimal enabling disclosure, making them weak as offensive prior art but useful as anti-claim-scope ammunition for any cartridge integrator to cite as evidence that broad cartridge claims are not novel. Companion existing entry: theranos-promised-cartridge documents the marketing claim; this entry catalogs the asserted IP.
sources: Reuters and Bloomberg coverage of Fortress/Labrador BioFire suit 2020

ip_citations: US 6,258,540 (Non-invasive prenatal diagnosis - amplifying and detecting paternally-inherited cell-free fetal DNA from maternal plasma/serum) - held patent-ineligible under 35 U.S.C. Section 101 / Mayo against Prometheus
Related NIPT patents asserted/contested among Sequenom, Verinata (Illumina), Ariosa (Roche), Natera, Ravgen
notes: Wave 6 landmark litigation. The Section 101 case that struck the foundational NIPT patent.
prior_art_notes: The most cited diagnostics Section 101 case after Mayo and Myriad. Sequenom US 6,258,540 covered the foundational insight (Lo et al. 1997) that cell-free fetal DNA circulates in maternal plasma and can be amplified and detected non-invasively - the basis of all non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT). The Federal Circuit (788 F.3d 1371, 2015) held the claims patent-ineligible: the natural phenomenon (cffDNA in maternal plasma) plus only conventional amplification/detection steps was not significantly more under the Mayo/Alice framework. En banc rehearing was denied over notable concurrences lamenting the result, and the Supreme Court denied certiorari in 2016. The practical effect: NIPT became a crowded competitive field (Sequenom, Illumina/Verinata, Ariosa/Roche, Natera, etc.) because the gatekeeping method patent fell. For this corpus, the case is the canonical demonstration that disclosing a microfluidic/molecular diagnostic method that merely applies routine PCR/sequencing to a natural correlation does not yield enforceable claims - the device implementation, not the discovered correlation, is where defensible IP (and useful prior art) lives. Companion to SCOTUS Mayo/Myriad/Alice entries from earlier waves.

notable_capabilities: Atmospheric particle inlet with cyclonic and baffle dust separator protecting humidity, pressure, and air-temperature sensors

Cite against later patents claiming Mars-rated cyclone-plus-hydrophobic-membrane dust filters.

disclosure_citation: 10x Genomics, Inc. v. Parse Biosciences, Inc., U.S. District Court for the District of Delaware, Case No. 1:23-cv-00930 (filed 2023-08-23); related counterclaims and IPR petitions
prior_art_notes: Records the August 2023 D. Del. infringement action in which 10x Genomics asserted multiple GEM/Drop-seq-lineage patents against Parse's Evercode split-pool products. Material because: (a) the case raises the question whether instrument-free combinatorial indexing infringes patents directed to compartmentalized droplet-based single-cell workflows; (b) Parse's defenses and counterclaims drew on Rosenberg 2018 SPLiT-seq, Cao et al. 2017 sci-RNA-seq, and prior University of Washington academic disclosures as 102 prior art against 10x's claims; (c) the docket exposed claim-construction theory pertinent to whether 'partition' must be a physical droplet or can be a fixed cell. Useful for invalidity contentions and as evidence of state of the art at relevant priority dates.

notable_capabilities: first industry-association demonstrator: write/store/retrieve workflow standardized
Twist 9600-well silicon synth chip as write substrate
Western Digital data path + storage interface software
prior_art_notes: Industry-consortium demonstration of DNA storage interoperability. Twist Bioscience's 9600-well MEMS silicon DNA synthesis chip serves as the write substrate (the wells are micro-reactors for in-situ phosphoramidite synthesis); Western Digital provides the storage-system data-path layer (encoding, addressing, integrity check); commercial nanopore sequencing provides readback. Anticipates: standardized DNA data storage interfaces and addressing schemes; integration of MEMS DNA synthesis chips with industry-standard storage software stacks; the architectural pattern of separate write-substrate (silicon microwell array) + storage-system layer + read-substrate (nanopore) as the canonical DNA storage architecture.

The dispute (filed as of corpus write date) is part of the broader pattern of pregnancy-biomarker IP fights (cf. sequenom-vs-ariosa-section-101 on NIPT). For the corpus: a reminder that the enforceable IP is the specific validated biomarker panel + measurement method, not the clinical goal; and a marker that maternal-blood-derived predictive tests (protein-based and RNA-based) are an active and contested space. Relevant to microfluidic immunoassay and cfRNA-prep cartridges.
